title: Simple Harmonic Motion
short_intro: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a special type of periodic motion where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from a fixed equilibrium position and is directed towards that position. It forms the foundation for understanding oscillatory phenomena, wave propagation, and acoustics in classical mechanics.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Kinematics of SHM, displacement, velocity, acceleration equations, time period and frequency of mass-spring systems, simple pendulum, and energy conservation.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Phase and phase difference, composition of two SHM lines (orthogonal and parallel), angular harmonic oscillators, physical pendulum, torsional pendulum, and differential formulation.

prerequisites: Differential equations of second order with constant coefficients

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics and Differential Equation of SHM
bullets: Defined by the differential equation d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0, where ω is the angular frequency.
Displacement as a function of time is given by x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), where A is amplitude and φ is initial phase.
Acceleration is always directed towards the mean position and has a magnitude proportional to displacement.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Conservation in SHM
bullets: Potential energy (U) varies parabolically with displacement, given by U = (1/2)mω²x².
Kinetic energy (K) is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions, given by K = (1/2)mω²(A² - x²).
Total mechanical energy E = U + K = (1/2)mω²A² remains constant throughout the motion in the absence of damping.

concept_notes.heading: Simple and Physical Pendulums
bullets: A simple pendulum consists of a point mass suspended by a massless, inextensible string of length l, with time period T = 2π&sqrt;(l/g).
A physical (compound) pendulum is any rigid body oscillating about a horizontal axis, with T = 2π&sqrt;(I / mgd), where I is moment of inertia and d is distance from pivot to center of mass.
Kater's pendulum is a reversible pendulum used for the precise experimental determination of acceleration due to gravity (g).

concept_notes.heading: Superposition of Simple Harmonic Motions
bullets: Collinear SHMs of the same frequency combine to yield a single SHM whose amplitude depends on the phase difference between them.
Perpendicular SHMs of equal frequency combine to form circular or elliptical trajectories depending on the phase difference.
Lissajous figures are formed when two mutually perpendicular SHMs of different frequency ratios are superimposed.

derivations.title: Differential Equation and Time Period of Mass-Spring System
derivations.conditions: Horizontal frictionless surface, ideal spring obeying Hooke's law
steps: Apply Hooke's law for restoring force: F = -kx
Compare with standard SHM equation d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0 to get angular frequency ω = sqrt(k/m)

derivations.title: Time Period of a Simple Pendulum
derivations.conditions: Small amplitude approximation (θ << 1 radian), inextensible string
steps: Write the equation of torque about the point of suspension: τ = -mg l sin(θ)
Use rotational analogue of Newton's second law: I (d²θ/dt²) = -mgl sin(θ)
Substitute moment of inertia I = ml² and apply small angle approximation sin(θ) ≈ θ
Simplify to obtain ml² (d²θ/dt²) + mglθ = 0 or d²θ/dt² + (g/l)θ = 0
Determine angular frequency ω = sqrt(g/l) and time period T = 2π sqrt(l/g)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration vs. Time
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three synchronized sinusoidal curves plotted against time t, showing phase relationships (velocity leads displacement by π/2 radians, acceleration leads velocity by π/2 radians and is in antiphase with displacement).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Highlights the kinematic interrelationships and phase differences between displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual MCQs on phase relationships and reading maximum values.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential, Kinetic, and Total Energy vs. Displacement
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parabolic curves for potential energy symmetric about x = 0, inverted parabolic curve for kinetic energy, and a horizontal straight line representing constant total energy E at x = ±A.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates continuous interconversion between kinetic and potential energy while total mechanical energy remains conserved.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems involving energy values at specific displacements (e.g., when K = U).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Simple Pendulum Experiment (T² vs. l Graph)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight-line graph plotting T² on the y-axis against length l on the x-axis, passing through the origin.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight line equals 4π²/g, allowing experimental determination of g.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Practical viva and analytical graph-based numerical questions.

solved_numericals.question: A particle executes SHM with an amplitude of 5 cm and a frequency of 2 Hz. Calculate its maximum velocity and maximum acceleration.
solution_steps: Identify given values: A = 0.05 m, f = 2 Hz.
Calculate maximum velocity: v_max = Aω = 0.05 × 4π = 0.2π m s^-1 ≈ 0.628 m s^-1.
Calculate maximum acceleration: a_max = Aω² = 0.05 × (4π)² = 0.05 × 16π² = 0.8π² m s^-2 ≈ 7.89 m s^-2.

solved_numericals.question: At what displacement from the mean position is the kinetic energy of a simple harmonic oscillator equal to its potential energy? Given amplitude is A.
solution_steps: Write expression for kinetic energy: K = (1/2)mω²(A² - x²).
Write expression for potential energy: U = (1/2)mω²x².
Simplify equation: A² - x² = x^2 Rightarrow 2x² = A².

solved_numericals.question: A uniform slender rod of mass M and length L is pivoted at one end and allowed to oscillate as a physical pendulum in a vertical plane. Find its time period for small oscillations.
solution_steps: Identify moment of inertia of a uniform rod about one end: I = (1/3)ML².
Determine distance from pivot to center of mass: d = L/2.
Substitute I and d into the physical pendulum formula: T = 2π \sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Restoring force is strictly linear (F = -kx) which holds true only for small displacements within the elastic limit.
Damping forces (like air resistance or internal friction) are assumed to be zero unless explicitly stated otherwise in damped harmonic motion models.
For pendulums, angle θ must be small enough so that sin(θ) ≈ θ holds with negligible error.

common_misconceptions.wrong: SHM is the only type of periodic motion.
common_misconceptions.correct: All SHMs are periodic, but not all periodic motions are simple harmonic (e.g., planetary motion, motion of a simple clock pendulum with large amplitude).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Acceleration is zero at the extreme positions in SHM.
common_misconceptions.correct: Acceleration is maximum at the extreme positions and zero at the mean (equilibrium) position.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on its mass.
common_misconceptions.correct: The time period formula T = 2π \sqrt{l/g} is independent of the mass of the bob.
